nameStory: The Arcigera Flower Moth gets its name from its scientific species name 'arcigera,' which means 'bearing a bow' in Latin, likely referring to curved markings on its wings. Like many flower moths in the Schinia genus, it's called a 'flower moth' because adults are often found visiting flowers for nectar, and their caterpillars feed exclusively on specific flowering plants.
description: The Arcigera Flower Moth is a small, delicate moth with a wingspan of about an inch (22-25 mm across). These pretty moths belong to the large family of cutworm moths, though unlike their soil-dwelling cousins, these species are closely tied to flowers. Adults are active from midsummer through early fall, fluttering around aster flowers where they feed and lay their eggs. Their intricate wing patterns help them blend in perfectly among the blooms they depend on.

idTips.label: Wing span
idTips.description: Small moth with wings spanning just under an inch (22-25 mm) - about the size of a large thumbnail when spread

idTips.label: Habitat association
idTips.description: Found exclusively around wild asters and related flowers - if you see small moths visiting fall asters, look closer

idTips.label: Flight period
idTips.description: Active during late summer evenings from July through September - often comes to porch lights near wildflower areas

idTips.label: Body build
idTips.description: Delicate build typical of flower moths - more slender and refined-looking than the chunky cutworm moths in the same family

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings tent-like over body rather than spread flat, creating a triangular silhouette

habitat: Look for Arcigera Flower Moths in open areas where wild asters grow abundantly - old fields, prairie remnants, roadsides, and meadow edges. They're particularly common in areas with smooth blue aster, purple-stemmed aster, and aromatic aster. You'll find them from sea level to moderate elevations throughout New England, wherever their host plants thrive in sunny, well-drained soils.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active yet - look for dried stems of last year's asters where eggs may have overwintered.
seasonality.summer: Adults begin emerging in July, becoming most active in late summer evenings around blooming asters and other late-season wildflowers.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity continues through September with moths actively feeding and mating around fall aster blooms before cold weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - the species overwinters as eggs or early larval stages on dried aster stems.

funFact: Arcigera Flower Moth caterpillars are so specialized that they can only survive on a handful of aster species - but here's the amazing part: the adult female moths can somehow detect the exact chemical signature of the right aster species from among dozens of similar-looking plants, ensuring their babies land on the perfect dinner table every time.
confusionNotes: Many small moths visit flowers at night, but Arcigera Flower Moths are specifically tied to asters - if you're not seeing them around wild asters, you're probably looking at a different species. The key memory trick: 'Aster-lovers' - these moths live and die by aster flowers.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'cutworm moths' for this family can be confusing since flower moths like this species don't cut plants at all - they're named after other family members whose caterpillars cut through plant stems. Flower moths are actually the 'well-behaved' members of this large moth family.
compareHints: The closely related Primrose Moth (Schinia florida) is very similar but feeds on evening primroses instead of asters - if you find small flower moths around yellow evening primrose blooms rather than purple/white aster flowers, you've likely found the primrose species instead. Both are small and delicate, but their plant associations are the best way to tell them apart.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The closely related Arcigera Flower Moth (Schinia arcigera) is the most similar species in the same genus found in New England.
